slides.title: TCP Header Going Inside Every Field
slides.body:
What Each One Actually Does?
Sequence Number
Four fields that drive everything in TCP:
Acknowledgment Number
Control Flags
Window Size

slides.title: RFC 793 vs Modern TCP
slides.body:
Flag Field History
RFC
Reserved
RFC 793 (1981) — Original
6 bits
Control Bits
3 bits
Modern (post RFC 3168)
6 bits: URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, FIN only
9 bits: NS*, CWR, ECE added for ECN

slides.title: TCP Control Flags
slides.body:
All 9 Flags
SYN(Synchronize)
Flag
Initiates connection, exchanges ISN, consumes 1 sequence number
What it does ?
Only on the first packet from each side
When Used ?
ACK(Acknowledge)
Confirms receipt. Makes the Ack Number field valid
Every packet except the first SYN
FIN(Finish)
Graceful close: No more data, in-transit data delivered first
When an endpoint is done sending

slides.title: TCP Control Flags
slides.body:
All 9 Flags
RST(Reset)
Flag
Abruptly terminates connection, in-transit data may be lost
What it does ?
Errors, port unreachable, invalid segments
When Used ?
PSH(Push)
Tells receiver to deliver data immediately to app, skip buffering
Data segments needing immediate delivery
URG(Urgent)
When sender marks data as urgent
Marks bytes as urgent, processed before buffered data, activates Urgent Pointer field

slides.title: TCP Control Flags
slides.body:
All 9 Flags
CWR(Congestion Window Reduced)
Flag
Sender confirms it received ECE and has already reduced sending rate
What it does ?
Next new data packet after receiving an ECE-flagged ACK
When Used ?
ECE(ECN-Echo)
Handshake: advertises ECN support. Data transfer: signals congestion detected
SYN (negotiation) and ACKs when CE-marked IP packet received
NS*(Nonce Sum)
Not used
Experimental, protection against hidden congestion signals. Deprecated 2017

slides.title: Sequence Numbers & Acknowledgment Numbers
slides.body: Sequence Numbers & Acknowledgment Numbers

slides.title: Sequence Numbers
slides.body:
How TCP Tracks Every Byte of Data?
The Sequence Number field (32 bits) identifies the position of the first byte of data in this segment within the total byte stream being sent
How Sequence Numbers Work:
Each side independently picks a random 32-bit Initial Sequence Number (ISN) at connection start, not 0

slides.title: Sequence Numbers
slides.body:
How TCP Tracks Every Byte of Data
Why random? 
Sequence Number advances by the exact number of bytes sent in that segment
SYN and FIN each consume exactly 1 sequence number, even though they carry no application data

slides.title: Sequence Numbers
slides.body:
How TCP Tracks Every Byte of Data
This is why the ACK after a SYN is always ISN + 1

slides.title: Sequence Numbers
slides.body:
What Sequence Numbers Enable
Ordering
Out-of-order segments are reordered and reassembled correctly at the receiver
Duplicate Detection
The duplicate Sequence Number is identified and the second copy is discarded
Loss Detection
A gap in sequence numbers indicates missing bytes that must be retransmitted

slides.title: Sequence Numbers
slides.body:
Analogy
Page numbers in a book delivered one chapter at a time
Even if Chapter 5 arrives before Chapter 3, page numbers allow correct reassembly
If Chapter 4 never arrives, the reader knows exactly which chapter to request

slides.title: Acknowledgment Numbers
slides.body:
How Receiver Confirms Delivery?
Acknowledgment Number = Last byte received + 1
This is a Cumulative Acknowledgment, it confirms all bytes up to (but not including) the Ack Number have been received correctly, the Ack Number is only valid when the ACK flag = 1

slides.title: Acknowledgment Numbers
slides.body: How the Receiver Confirms Delivery

The receiver keeps sending Ack=1201

slides.title: ACKs in TCP
slides.body:
Cumulative Acknowledgment
One Ack number confirms ALL bytes received up to that point
Ack=1401 - "Received everything up to byte 1400,         send me 1401 next"
If byte 1201 is lost,  receiver keeps repeating Ack=1201 even if later bytes arrived
Cumulative ACK

slides.title: ACKs in TCP
slides.body:
Piggybacking
When the receiver has data to send back, the ACK is bundled with that outgoing segment
No separate ACK packet needed
Saves one packet per exchange
Piggybacking

slides.title: Piggybacking
slides.body:
Working of Piggybacking
HOST ‘A’
HOST ‘B’
HOST ‘A’ sends data
HOST ‘B’ sends data along with the acknowledgment of data received by A
HOST ‘A’ sends only ACK (when there is no data to send)
Time

slides.title: Piggybacking
slides.body:
Delayed ACK
TCP waits up to 200ms before sending a pure ACK, hoping to piggyback it
If nothing to attach after 200ms ACK is sent alone
Delayed ACK

slides.title: How Much Data Can Be In Flight at Once?
slides.body:
Flow Control
institute_id
Window Size (16 bits) 
How many bytes the receiver can accept right now without waiting for individual ACKs. This is TCP Flow Control

slides.title: Window Size
slides.body:
Flow Control
Advertised in every ACK, dynamic, changes throughout the connection
Sender cannot exceed Window Size bytes of unACKed data in flight
Window Size = 0 → sender stops completely

slides.title: Window Size
slides.body:

Sent & ACKed

Can Send

As ACKs arrive, left boundary slides right, new bytes enter the "Can Send" zone

slides.title: Window Size
slides.body:
Sliding Window
Max Window Size :
65,535 bytes (16-bit limit)
Window Scaling (RFC 7323):
For high-speed/high-latency links where 65 KB in flight is not enough
Shift count 0–14 negotiated in SYN Options
Effective window = Window Size × 2^(shift count), Max ≈ 1 GB
Both sides must agree, if only one sends it, scaling is not used
